turns.response_html:
It sounds like you're describing a "stack and nest" container design. While the term "boom bin" is specifically used in the mycological community for mushroom cultivation (as a modified monotub), the physical design of two tubs nesting or stacking is a standard industrial container type found across many sectors.

In industrial and commercial settings, these are often called "Stack and Nest Totes" or "Cross-Stack Tubs."

Why they look like "two tubs"

The design you're seeing usually serves two distinct functional states:

  • Stacking (Full): When you rotate the bins 90° or 180° (depending on the specific brand design), they sit securely on the rim of the bin below. This prevents them from sliding and allows you to build vertical columns.
  • Nesting (Empty): When you rotate the bins back to their original alignment, the tapered walls allow one bin to drop inside the one below it. This reduces the empty storage footprint by as much as 75–80%, which is critical for shipping efficiency and warehouse space.

Where to find them on the open market

You don't need a specialized "grow" supply shop to get these. They are commodities in industrial logistics. You can find them under these categories:

  • "Stack and Nest Totes": These are the most common industrial versions. You can find them through industrial supply retailers like Simplastics, Uline, or Global Industrial.
  • "Distribution Totes" or "Attached Lid Containers": If your "boom bin" has an attached, hinged lid, look for these. These are the standard bins used by companies like Amazon or grocery delivery services to transport inventory.
  • "Agricultural/Food Grade Tubs": If you need them for safe food or substrate handling, look for ones labeled "FDA-approved" or "food-grade polypropylene." These are frequently used in commercial kitchens and bakeries.

A quick tip for your search: If you are looking for that specific "two-tub" aesthetic (usually a clear or translucent plastic), searching for "clear stack and nest totes" will usually lead you to the exact type of hardware used by the hobbyists who coined the "boom bin" term. Many of them are simply sourcing standard heavy-duty industrial storage bins (often made by companies like ORBIS or Buckhorn) and modifying them with drilled holes or custom gaskets.

Since you are already comfortable with hardware projects and 3D printing custom components, you might find that buying the standard industrial "stack and nest" totes and DIY-ing your own "boom" modifications (like adding bulkhead fittings for humidity or custom-printed gaskets) will be significantly cheaper than buying a branded "mushroom" kit.

turns.response_html:
You are entirely correct. Pre-fabricated mushroom monotubs like the Boomr Bin or specialized kits can carry a significant markup compared to the raw materials.

A standard brand-name monotub kit typically runs between $30 to $65 for just the plastic tub itself, while fully automated versions can cost upwards of $270. In comparison, heavy-duty industrial or consumer storage containers of similar volume usually cost between $10 to $20.

By purchasing standard tubs and converting them yourself, you can build a fleet of custom enclosures for a fraction of the price.

What to Look For in an Open-Market Tub

When searching consumer marketplaces for DIY alternatives, look for these specific attributes to mimic a professional design:

  • Material: Opt for Heavy-Duty Polypropylene (PP). It is highly durable, flexible enough to drill without cracking, and easy to sanitize.
  • Clarity: A clear or translucent lid and upper body is crucial to allow ambient light in, which triggers and guides mushroom fruiting direction.
  • The "Two-Tub" Effect (The Base): Many growers prefer a black or opaque base (or they use a dark plastic liner). This blocks light from reaching the sides and bottom of the substrate, which directly prevents "side pinning"—mushrooms growing squished against the plastic wall where they are difficult to harvest and prone to rotting.

Recommended Consumer Alternatives for DIY Builds

Here are the best high-volume consumer tubs widely available on the open market that make excellent DIY bases:

Large Scale Builds (50–60+ Quarts)

These match the 22" x 15" footprint of premium commercial bins and provide enough depth for a substantial 3-to-4-inch substrate bed plus plenty of vertical fruiting headspace.

The Sterilite 66 Quart Storage Tote is the absolute gold standard for DIY monotub builders. It is inexpensive, widely accessible, and features secure gaskets/latches.

  • Why it works: The deep walls provide excellent airflow stratification, and the clear plastic provides perfect visibility. The indexing on the lid also makes them safely stackable when you run multiple bins.

Compact / Space-Saving Builds (30–40 Quarts)

If you are working in limited vertical space or prefer running smaller, isolated batches to mitigate the risk of cross-contamination, a shallower mid-sized bin is ideal.

The Sterilite 32-Quart Clear Latching Storage Tote gives you the exact same footprint and latch mechanism as the larger version but at half the height.

  • Why it works: It fits easily on standard wire shelving units. Because it is shallower, it requires less automated air management to clear out heavy carbon dioxide pools at the base.

Price Comparison: DIY vs. Branded Kits

To see how the economics stack up, here is a direct look at using standard consumer hardware versus buying purpose-built mycology bins:

Tips for Modifying Your Consumer Totes

Since you are prepping these from scratch, a few quick fabrication tips will save you from ruining the plastic:

  1. Avoid Standard Drill Bits: Standard twist drill bits can easily catch on polypropylene and crack the tub walls. Use a step drill bit (unibit) or a sharp hole saw running at medium speed to cut clean 1-inch or 2-inch ventilation holes.
  2. Air Exchange Placement: Drill your lower holes right above where the top of your substrate line will sit (usually about 4–5 inches up from the bottom) to let heavy $CO_2$ escape. Place your upper holes near the top of the lid or high on the side walls to let fresh oxygen draft in.
  3. Filtration: You can buy sheets of adhesive synthetic filter discs online very cheaply, or simply pack the drilled holes with standard polyester fiberfill (polyfil) to allow clean gas exchange while keeping out wild spores and contaminants.

When comparing specialized bin stores in the Des Moines metro (like The Container Store in West Des Moines or industrial suppliers like Iowa-Des Moines Supply) against big-box giants like Menards, Walmart, or Dollar General, it comes down to a trade-off between rock-bottom pricing and structural variety.

For a custom project where you need straightforward, modification-friendly plastic, mass-market retailers are significantly more cost-effective. Here is how the marketplace dynamics break down:

Big Box Retailers (Walmart, Menards, Dollar General)

Verdict: The most cost-effective option for basic builds. If you just need a standard clear enclosure to drill into, big-box stores crush the specialty market on raw unit price because they buy consumer plastic in massive volume.

  • Walmart: They consistently offer the lowest baseline price for standard consumer plastic. For instance, a single Sterilite 66-Quart Latching Tote runs under $10 in-store, which is tough to beat anywhere else.
  • Menards: While slightly more expensive than Walmart for basic clear bins, Menards has a much better selection of heavy-duty industrial totes (like the solid black or yellow-lid tough boxes). If you want a thicker polymer that can handle more physical wear, their utility section is excellent.
  • Dollar General: Good for very small, compact shoe-box-sized builds, but they lack the large-volume 30–60+ quart inventory needed for substantial vertical builds.

Specialty & Specialty Industrial Stores (Des Moines Metro)

Verdict: Not competitive on price, but highly competitive on variety and dimensions.

  • The Container Store (Mills Civic Parkway, WDM): Walking in here will give you every physical variation imaginable—extra-deep bins, long narrow profiles, and varying clarity options. However, you pay a heavy premium for aesthetics and organization engineering. A specialized modular bin here can easily cost $15 to $35+ for equivalent volumes that cost $9 at Walmart.
  • Industrial Supply Houses (e.g., Iowa-Des Moines Supply): These places deal in commercial-grade packaging and logistics hardware. They are incredibly competitive if you are buying a commercial pallet pack of heavy-duty, commercial-grade cross-stack totes or distribution containers. However, for a small batch of 2 to 6 tubs, their single-unit retail pricing or minimum-order requirements usually make them impractical for a casual hobbyist.

Summary Strategy

If your goal is to minimize cost per enclosure, stick to Walmart or Menards. You can walk out with several massive 66-quart clear containers for the price of a single specialized bin from a high-end organizer store. The raw plastic functions exactly the same once modified.
